definition: TakeSix is an open format and libraries that let an AI agent answer with a diagram you can click into instead of a wall of text: at most six blocks per screen, and any block opens into up to six more.

faq.a: TakeSix is an open format and libraries that let an AI agent answer with a diagram you can click into instead of a wall of text: at most six blocks per screen, and any block opens into up to six more. The gist of the answer fits on the first screen; the reader clicks a block for depth, and long text opens next to the block that needs it.

faq.q: How do I get TakeSix diagrams from my AI agent?
faq.a: Connect the MCP server @takesix/mcp (for example, in Claude Code: claude mcp add --scope user takesix -- npx -y @takesix/mcp), or install the Agent Skill from the takesix-agent repository. Then ask for an overview, a plan or an architecture "as a TakeSix diagram". It works with Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, Cursor, VS Code and other MCP clients.

faq.q: How is TakeSix different from Mermaid?
faq.a: Mermaid turns a text description into one flat picture, and a big subject makes a big, crowded picture. A TakeSix diagram is a tree of screens: each screen has at most six blocks, and any block opens into its own screen. The format is JSON made for agents to write: a validator lists every problem with its place in the file, so the agent fixes its own answer.

faq.q: How is TakeSix different from the C4 model?
faq.a: C4 is a way to describe software architecture at four fixed levels: context, containers, components and code. TakeSix is a general format: any subject, as many levels as it needs, and a hard limit of six blocks per screen. A C4 model fits into TakeSix well; the architecture blueprint of the agent skill follows the same idea of zooming in.

faq.q: How is TakeSix different from draw.io or Excalidraw?
faq.a: draw.io and Excalidraw are drawing tools: a person places shapes on a canvas by hand. In TakeSix an agent writes the diagram as JSON and places blocks on a 6×6 grid, so there are no coordinates to tune and every diagram reads the same way. A person can still open and change it in the TakeSix editor.

A reader takes in a handful of things at a glance. Six blocks are enough to say the whole thing on one screen and few enough to read without scrolling. When a subject needs more, it gets another level, not a bigger screen.
A .takesix.json file and one self-contained HTML file that opens in any browser, without internet. In apps that support MCP Apps, such as Claude Desktop, the diagram also opens right in the chat.

faq.q: Is it free, and where does my data go?
faq.a: TakeSix is open source under the MIT license. The MCP server and the skill run on your computer; the diagrams are not sent anywhere. The editor on takesix.vapnik.de also works in the browser only.
